back: A graph of the temperature of a substance against time as it is heated steadily. Flat sections show changes of state.

front: On the heating curve of a pure solid, what do the first and second flat sections show?
back: First (lower) flat section: melting, at the melting point. Second (higher) flat section: boiling, at the boiling point.

front: **Supplement.** Why does the temperature stay constant while a pure solid melts or a pure liquid boils?
back: The energy supplied is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles, not to increase their kinetic energy.

front: **Supplement.** Why does the temperature stay constant while a liquid freezes on a cooling curve?
back: Energy is given out as the particles are pulled into fixed positions, and this balances the energy lost to the surroundings.

front: Which states are present during melting, and which during boiling?
back: Melting: solid and liquid together. Boiling: liquid and gas together.

front: **Supplement.** Why is the boiling section of water's heating curve longer than the melting section?
back: Boiling separates the particles completely, which needs much more energy than melting, where the particles only start to slide past each other.

front: How do the freezing point and the melting point of a pure substance compare?
back: They are the same temperature: the flat section of the cooling curve is at the melting point.

front: What happens to the particles on a **rising** section of a heating curve?
back: They gain kinetic energy and move (or vibrate) faster, so the temperature rises. Only one state is present.

front: Give three good practices when recording a cooling curve.
back: Read the temperature at regular intervals with a stop-watch; stir so the whole sample is at one temperature; read the thermometer at eye level. (Melt the solid in a water bath, not a naked flame.)

front: Why does pure water boil at about $95\ ^\circ\text{C}$ in Harare?
back: Harare is about 1 500 m above sea level, so the air pressure is lower; boiling points fall when the pressure falls. ($100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is the boiling point at sea-level pressure.)
